Twenty-First Century Psychoanalysis, Thomas Svolos. London: Karnac, 2017. 294 pp.

Cassandra Seltman

Cassandra Seltman

Cassandra Seltman  

In Twenty-First Century Psychoanalysis Thomas Svolos presents a collection of his work from the early 2000s, essays and lectures broadly covering issues of diagnosis, countertransference, medication, addiction, the body, psychosis, fantasy, and of course what brings us to treatment—the symptom. Svolos denies psychoanalysis as a system, and therefore the book is not systematic. He opens with the wager that if a form of psychoanalysis is to survive in the twenty-first century, it will be a Lacanian psychoanalysis.

Svolos examines how the encounter of psychoanalysis with postmodernity in the 1960s changed the relationship of theory to the symptom. Should the symptom be read? Perhaps celebrated and enjoyed, as Deleuze suggests? At this time the culture industry is diagnosed, labeled “late capitalism,” the term popularized by Marxist and activist Ernest Mandel, and picked up by twentieth-century critical theorists belonging to the Frankfurt school, Theodor Adorno and Fredric Jameson. Late capitalism, although like all broad labels varying in meaning and connotation, generally suggests a movement away from any possibility of socialism and a reinforcement of the domination of the economy over our bodies and minds. The phrase has seen renewed interest in the past decade, picked up more broadly outside of neo-Marxists and critical theorists.

K. Branche   Finishing studies for his MA at The New School for Social Research. His main interests include the intersections between psychoanalysis and art, politics, and cultural trends, with an interest in psychoanalysis as a development of western thought, specifically. He sees a particular value in its investigations of the unconscious as identifying otherwise neglected aspects of that tradition, including weaknesses as well as strengths.

Basing his original thought chiefly in Freud's Beyond the Pleasure Principle, the author seeks to establish a theory and philosophy of artistic production as arising from the compulsion to repeat, and as first expressed in the near-universal tendency of children to intentionally re-create and repeat traumatic experiences in safety as a way of achieving mastery of the feelings engendered by them.

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst  

This slim volume is part of the New Library of Psychoanalysis series sponsored by the Institute of Psychoanalysis, London, currently under the general editorship of Alessandra Lemma. The stated aim of this series is to promote mutual understanding among psychoanalysts and specialists in other fields (philosophy, social science, literature and the arts, etc.). In the process, the series also brings together what sometimes seem to be divergent approaches of Anglo-American and Continental European thinkers.

The book is a newly published English translation of a 2014 work by Laurence Kahn, former president of the French Psychoanalytic Association. At first glance, the reader might expect to be presented with a simple summary or overview of contemporary psychoanalytic theory or practice, with some connections drawn to the broader cultural or literary milieu. The book is succinct, yet deceptively profound.

Elizabeth Severn: The “Evil Genius” of Psychoanalysis. Arnold William Rachman. London and New York: Routledge, 2018. 332 pp.

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall  

Arnold Rachman's book is important. It is not only a mighty contribution to the history of psychoanalysis but clarifies Sandor Ferenczi's groundbreaking therapy with Elizabeth Severn while deepening our understanding of the relationship between Ferenczi and Spotnitz.

Arnold Rachman's Prologue

Rachman immediately helps us emotionally understand the basis of his elegant inquiry by presenting personal anecdotes of his life and professional history. Thus, he demonstrates important aspects of Ferenczi's clinical approach: openness, flexibility, judicious self-disclosure, and humanity. From the standpoint of his training in clinical psychology at the University of Chicago, he announces his respect for Carl Rogers' mantra of empathy, positive regard, and genuine reflection—all of which Rachman finds in Ferenczi and Severn. He supplies vignettes of his being rejected which are reminiscent of Ferenczi's travails.

Announcement from the Editor

Faye Newsome

Faye Newsome

Faye Newsome  

It has been an honor to serve as the editor of Modern Psychoanalysis, following in the footsteps of Phyllis Meadow and June Bernstein. It was Meadow's vision that gave birth to the journal in 1976 and Bernstein's dedication that sustained that vision. I owe a debt of gratitude to each of them for their guidance and encouragement during their lifetimes.

This issue has been co-edited by William J. Hurst and me. I will now step aside, and beginning with the next issue it will be Dr. Hurst, who is a psychoanalyst, writer, and philosopher, whose professional expertise and depth of erudition will ensure the journal's continuance and flourishing, presenting the ideas that modern psychoanalysts develop as they do their clinical work.

Faye Newsome

The Upaya of Modern Psychoanalysis

Edward Jones

Edward Jones

16 West 10th Street
New York, NY 10011
Email: edward@nowyogany.com

Edward Jones   Received his master's degree from NYGSP and is engaged in psychoanalytic training at CMPS. He has taught meditation and yoga for fifteen years, in New York City and internationally. His interest in Buddhist psychology has been invigorated by a recognition of its synergy with psychoanalytic theory. Mr. Jones has been a featured presenter at the Rubin Museum of Art, in the pages of Real Simple magazine, and at the Madeleine L'Engle Conference. He is one of the founders of Now Yoga, a Buddhist-oriented vinyasa yoga school in New York, where he teaches regularly.

The author finds significant commonality between a central concept of Buddhist practice and one that characterizes modern psychoanalytic theory and technique. Upaya, or “skillful means,” forms the basis for many of that spiritual tradition's assumptions about how to approach individual and universal suffering. Put simply, an Upaya is any intervention that aims to achieve a practical, worldly effect and is guided not by adherence to a specific praxis but instead is oriented toward the particular circumstances of the subject upon whom it is being applied. The modern psychoanalytic technique of joining the patient's resistance is harmonious with Upaya in that treatment is adapted to suit the psychic reality of the patient, and prioritizes emotional experience and self-generated interpretation rather than analyst interpretation or intellectual insight.

Joshua Aguayo

Joshua Aguayo

Joshua Aguayo  

British Psychoanalysis: New Perspectives in the Independent Tradition is perhaps a book that, much like George Makari's Revolution in Mind, seeks to reexamine a period in psychoanalytic history, with the intent to mine new revelations from our shared pasts. Psychoanalyst, editor and author Gregorio Kohon expertly explores the vicissitudes and complexities of the “independent tradition” in British psychoanalysis, along with the stable of preeminent British psychoanalysts, such as Winnicott, Bollas, and Khan, around whom it took shape.

Early Childhood Development in the Independent Tradition

After Kohon's introductory remarks, the reader is thrown into one of the theoretical conflicts that gave rise to the independent tradition, that around the early development of the child. Winnicott, Khan, Bollas and Cohen discuss successes and failures in the child's early environment following the atemporality of the unconscious as a means to guide them. Spotnitz in Seoul: Applying Modern Psychoanalysis in South Korea

Joon Lee PsyaD

Joon Lee

1581 Beacon Street
Brookline, MA 02446
Email: drjoonholee@gmail.com

Joon Lee   Faculty member of the Hanshin University Graduate School of Psychoanalysis and is co-director of the Korean Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis and the Gwanghwamun Psychotherapy Center in Seoul. He is the translator of the Korean edition of Hyman Spotnitz's Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic Patient.

The author considers the popularity of modern psychoanalytic ideas in Seoul, Korea, and argues that the modern psychoanalytic conceptualization of aggression turned inward, as in the narcissistic defense, resonates with Koreans on both a cultural/social and an individual level. Examples, including events and phenomena known as Hwa-byung, Han, Suicide, and Korean Air 801, are given to portray destructive self-attacks in contemporary Korea. Furthermore, the author shares his experience teaching and practicing psychoanalysis in Seoul to examine the use of the narcissistic defense as particular to Korean society and culture.

Milena Cornick PsyaD LCSW

Milena Cornick   Graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) in New York. She received her doctorate from the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP). Dr. Cornick is member of the faculty, a training analyst, supervisor and advisor at CMPS and the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (NYGSP). She is in private practice in New York.

A sixty-three year-old woman formed a transference that appeared to be affected by her identical twinship, and which seemed to play a part in repetitive negative patterns, including intense and frequent treatment-destructive behaviors. The patient sought tirelessly to be joined with the analyst in a relationship that resembled the one she reported sharing with her twin, but also yearned to be separate from her twin. This conflict was realized in the transference as she oscillated between attempting to create and to destroy a twinship relationship with the analyst.

Adrienne Harris

80 University Place, 5th floor

Adrienne Harris   Faculty member and supervisor in the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis. She is on the faculty and is a supervisor at the Psychoanalytic Institute of Northern California and is an editor of Psychoanalytic Dialogues and of Studies In Gender and Sexuality. She is an editor of the book series Relational Perspectives in Psychoanalysis, and an editor of the IPA e-journal psychoanalysis today. In 2009, she was a founder of the Sandor Ferenczi Center at the New School.

Introduction

Over the preceding year, I have written, rewritten, and rethought the question of sexual harassment and #MeToo. I have, like many people, I imagine, been shocked and deeply engaged with these issues, in talks and emails and readings, watching the landscape change, progress, and backslide. I find myself changing and editing and reworking on an almost weekly basis. #MeToo as movement and as social force and deep problematic has undergone many rapid transformations. It seems also to have provoked powerful generational differences in responsiveness, in addition to the more obvious differences in gender and identity positions.

This paper was first presented at the CMPS Annual Conference Us, Them, and #MeToo: Psychoanalysis, Feminism, and the Legacy of History. November 17, 2018.

Pain: A Psychoanalytic Study in the Etiology of Depressive Disorders

Paolo Azzone MD

Paolo Azzone

Via Statuto 9 20020
Lainate, Milan, Italy
Email: paoloazzone@hotmail.com
Telephone +390262069055

Paolo Azzone   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst. He is head of the Forensic Psychiatric Patients Program at the ASST-Rhodense Hospital in Milan, Italy. Dr. Azzone substantially contributed to the establishment of a psychotherapy research tradition in Italy, with empirical studies on the psychotherapy process and on dreams. His current interests include psychoanalytic treatment of depression and the intersections between psychoanalysis and philosophy, history, and religious experience. He is co-editor of La mente dell'anima (The Mind of Soul), 2008, and the author of Depression as a Psychoanalytic Problem, 2012.

The author considers that, in what we might characterize as this neuroscience era, we risk underestimating Freud's fundamental contribution to the understanding of depressive conditions. He proposes that the development of object relations theory, and particularly Bion's introduction of mental pain as a core element of psychoanalysis, can enable us to more fully appreciate the revolutionary quality of the interpersonal insights included in Freud's Mourning and Melancholia. Within the field of depressive disorders especially, the question of etiology may be elusive. Here we will rather try to formulate a constellation of interpersonal and intrapsychic events that we have met with notable regularity in psychoanalytic work with patients suffering from clinically significant depression. We can summarize them as follows: a) manifest symptoms of depression that can best be conceptualized as representations of an excess of mental pain within the psychic apparatus; b) depressed patients typically display enhanced susceptability to projections from a powerful core love object; c) the resulting excess of mental pain elicits intense aggression, and d) through the mechanism of object introjection, aggression is turned inward, toward the self.

The author reflects on the emergence of widespread new awareness of sexual and gender attitudes and dynamics on two distinct fronts. On the one hand, new insight into and growing condemnation of sexual harassment and intimidation; on the other and on a seemingly parallel path, an increasing awareness of transgender experience. She contemplates these movements as a psychoanalytic, feminist and literary critic.

Lucy Holmes   Licensed psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City, and a member of the faculties of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS), The New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (NYGSP) and the Center for Group Studies. A former president of the Society for Modern Psychoanalysis, she lectures widely on female development and the technique of modern psychoanalytic group analysis. A third book, a collection of papers on women and groups (one of which won the Gradiva Award in 2002), is in preparation.

Old age is a crisis in the life cycle which involves an unavoidable confrontation with human transience and an identity crisis similar to the angst of adolescence. Old people often experience hypochondria, depression and a surge of narcissism. Though psychoanalysis is more respectful of the elderly than are many professional communities, institutes and their communities struggle to deal with luminaries who show signs of cognitive decline or are dealing with a terminal illness. This paper considers the question of how termination with the aging analyst can be handled therapeutically. It also considers a few advantages of aging and techniques to cope with its challenges. The crucial need for objects to project onto and identify with is emphasized.

Frances Bigda-Peyton   Graduate of Harvard College. She received her master's degree from Harvard and her doctorate from Boston University. She serves as a training analyst, research advisor, and faculty member at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP). Her interests include couples therapy, the mind-body interface, framing analysis, and environmental activism. Dr. Bigda-Peyton's prior publications include When Drives are Dangerous: Drive Theory and Resource Overconsumption, and An Analysis of Intense Enactments in the Case of a 10-Year-Old Girl.

The author reflects on her psychoanalytic work with an especially challenging couple, intelligent and articulate but emotionally primitive. Emphasis is placed on creating personal safety, processing destructive attacks immediately, joining, using induced feelings and object-oriented questions, and encouraging something new to happen in the room to disrupt and expand entrenched dynamics. The question of concurrent, individual therapy is also discussed. The couples therapist works to create a “thirdness” where reflection, embodied communication, and maturation can unfold.

The Art of Personality in Literature and Psychoanalysis. Meg Harris Williams. London: Karnac Books Ltd., 2018. 248 pp.

Esra Atamer

Esra Atamer

Esra Atamer  

“In what sense can the shaping of personality be considered art?” asks Meg Harris Williams in the preface to her recent book. Her work performs a response to this question as she explores her own lineage with the post-Kleinian analysts and their philosophical fellows in her reading of diverse literary texts from ancient to modern times. Seeking the truth of one's own becoming is emphasized as an inherently poetic process throughout the book. This undercurrent theme finds its philosophical course through John Keats' negative capability, S⊘ren Kierkegaard's faith, and Wilfred Bion's the unknown.

Harris Williams interweaves an organic net of literary, philosophical, and psychoanalytic concepts and examples, in search of an aesthetic organization of the psyche toward selfhood. She stresses the role of curiosity-to-know as one of the driving forces in seeking one's psychic truth, as portrayed in the tragic hero's self-quest in ancient drama. For instance, the representations of the tragic hero's conflict in Aristotle and Keats are analytically described as the variants of Klein's epistemophilic drive, rooted in the ambivalence between love and hate felt toward the early objects.
